Predict from a fitted model

Source: R/model-classes.R, R/model-rf.R
spatial_fit-predict.Rd

predict() has a method for each backend: a random forest (rf_fit), a GWR (gwr_fit) and a Bayesian GP (bayesian_fit) fit. Every method reads newdata the same way: a layer without a CRS is read the way the training data were (see "Layers without a CRS" in spatialkit-geometry), the layer is transformed to the CRS used at fitting time, a feature that is not a point is reduced to one, and a row with a missing or non-finite predictor or no location gets NA. A layer that mixes XY with XYZ or XYM geometries is read in x and y. The response need not be present. With newdata = NULL each method returns the fit's own fitted values: out-of-bag predictions for a random forest, in-sample values for the others.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'gwr_fit'
predict(object, newdata = NULL, se.fit = FALSE, ...)

# S3 method for class 'bayesian_fit'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  summary = c("mean", "median"),
  type = c("epred", "predict"),
  draws = FALSE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'rf_fit'
predict(object, newdata = NULL, ...)

Arguments

object

A fitted rf_fit, gwr_fit or bayesian_fit.

newdata

An sf object carrying the predictors, or NULL for the fitted values.

se.fit

GWR only. Logical; also return standard errors. Default FALSE.

...

For a random forest, passed to ranger's predict method; any other name is an error. Arguments that make ranger return a matrix (predict.all = TRUE, type = "quantiles", type = "se" with predict.all) are refused, because the method returns one number per row; call predict(fit$engine, data = ...) for those. What ranger itself refuses, such as type = "quantiles" on a forest grown without quantreg = TRUE, is an error that gives ranger's reason. seed defaults to a constant, so the number of predict() calls a script makes (through predict_surface()'s chunk_size, say) does not shift later random draws; it does not change a regression forest's predictions. num.threads defaults to getOption("mc.cores", 1L). For a GWR or a Bayesian GP fit, not used: any argument here is an error, so a misspelt newdata cannot slip through.

summary

Bayesian GP only. "mean" (default) or "median" over the posterior draws.

type

Bayesian GP only. "epred" (default) for the expected value, without observation noise, or "predict" for posterior predictive draws, with it.

draws

Bayesian GP only. TRUE returns the full matrix of posterior draws instead of a summary. Default FALSE.

Value

For a random forest, a numeric vector aligned to nrow(newdata), with NA for rows dropped as incomplete (all NA, with a WARN line in the log, when every row is). The forest in fit$engine predicts (y - fit$info$response_centre) / fit$info$response_scale (see the Value section of fit_rf_model()); this method puts the centre and scale back. A failure inside ranger's predict method is an error.

For a GWR with se.fit = FALSE, a numeric vector aligned to nrow(newdata), with NA for rows dropped as missing or non-finite and for locations whose local regression cannot be estimated (see "When a GWR prediction is NA"). If the design matrix for newdata cannot be built, every value is NA and a warning says why. When the training data were read as longitude and latitude, a CRS-less newdata with an x outside -180 to 360 or a y beyond 90 north or south stops the call. With se.fit = TRUE, a list: fit (that vector), se.fit (the standard error of the fitted value, \(\hat\sigma\sqrt{s^\top s}\) with \(s\) the weights the local regression puts on the training responses), se.pred (the standard error of a new observation there, \(\hat\sigma\sqrt{1 + s^\top s}\), the square root of GWmodel::gwr.predict()'s prediction variance), residual.scale (\(\hat\sigma\), from the fit's residual sum of squares over its effective degrees of freedom) and df (those degrees of freedom). The standard errors treat the bandwidth as known and the local model as true at each location; they do not measure the bias of a local fit and are NA where the prediction is.

For a Bayesian GP fit, a numeric vector of length nrow(newdata), or an n_draws by nrow(newdata) matrix with draws = TRUE, in the units of the response (see "The response's centre and scale" in fit_bayesian_spatial_model()). Rows with a missing or non-finite predictor or coordinate, and rows carrying a level the model was not fitted with, are NA (an NA column with draws = TRUE). If the posterior draw fails the result is all NA (a one-row matrix for draws = TRUE) with a warning of class spatialkit_predict_failed that gives the cause. An ordinal or categorical family is an error under type = "epred": its expected value is a probability per response category. Use type = "predict", draws = TRUE for posterior draws of the predicted category, as category indices; the share of draws in each category estimates its probability. Without draws = TRUE, type = "predict" returns the mean (or median) category index, an expected rank for an ordinal family and an error for brms::categorical(), whose categories have no order. With newdata = NULL the cached fitted() values are returned only for the default summary = "mean", type = "epred", draws = FALSE; any other combination is recomputed against the training data, because the cache holds the expected values only.

Details

A random forest predicts with ranger's predict method. A GWR solves one local regression at each new location, with the fit's kernel and bandwidth (an adaptive bandwidth counts neighbours among the training points), and returns \(x^\top\hat\beta(u)\). The local regressions are weighted least squares solved by the pivoted QR fit_gwr_model() uses: on a window of full rank the values equal those of GWmodel::gwr.predict() to rounding error, and at a training location with that row's own predictors they equal fitted(). Each location stands alone, so one that cannot be estimated does not affect the others. A Bayesian GP fit applies the coordinate scaling and predictor standardisation stored at fit time and then calls brms::posterior_epred() or brms::posterior_predict().

Random forest predictors

A categorical predictor must not carry a level the forest was grown without, meaning a level with no training rows, not only one absent from levels(): an ordinary subset, or a spatial fold that holds out a whole class, keeps the unused level while the forest has no split for it. An unseen level is an error. A predictor that was numeric or logical when the forest was grown must arrive numeric or logical: ranger would otherwise code a character column as a factor and apply the numeric split thresholds to the codes, so a character column is refused. (ranger reads a logical as 0/1, so either form is accepted for one.)

When a GWR prediction is NA

A prediction is returned when it is estimable from the training points that carry weight at the new location, and is NA otherwise:

  • no training point carries weight there (a location beyond a fixed bisquare, tricube or boxcar bandwidth);

  • the training points in the window cannot place the new row: a predictor is constant among them at a value other than the new row's (a regional indicator, at a location whose window lies wholly in another region), or fewer of them carry weight than the new row needs.

Where a predictor is constant in the window at the new row's own value, its coefficient is not needed and the prediction is returned. The decision uses the rule and the tolerance of the fit (see "The local solve" in fit_gwr_model()). A warning of class "spatialkit_gwr_not_estimable" counts the NA predictions; it carries n_na, n and n_empty.

GWR locations beyond the reach of the fit

An adaptive bandwidth always finds its neighbours, and a Gaussian or an exponential kernel weights every training point, so a location far from the data still gets a number: the local regression of training points that are all far away, extrapolated. When a new location's nearest training point is farther than the widest kernel used at any training location reaches, the prediction is returned and a warning of class "spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation" counts those locations and gives the range of their distances. The widest kernel is the largest distance from a training point to its bandwidth-th nearest neighbour (object$info$max_kernel_width), or the bandwidth itself when it is fixed. A bisquare, tricube or boxcar kernel reaches as far as its width; a Gaussian or exponential kernel has no edge, and its reach is taken as three widths. The check is on distance alone and is lenient: a location just outside the data is not flagged. The warning carries n_far, n, reach and nearest (the smallest and largest distance to a nearest training point).

Each call raises the warning once, with its own counts. predict_surface(), cv_gwr(), cv_spatial(), cv_block_size_sweep() and select_features_forward() predict in pieces and raise one warning per call with the totals. A cross-validation gives the smallest and the largest reach among its folds, and a sweep counts a location once for each fit that put it out of reach. A loop of your own over predict() gets one warning per call; the example below totals them with a handler. To drop the warning where extrapolation is intended, use suppressWarnings(predict(fit, newdata), classes = "spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation").

Bayesian GP boundary

brms 2.17 to 2.22 do not store the Hilbert-space boundary \(L\) in a fitted GP basis, and recompute it from whatever rows predict() is handed. This method therefore appends two rows at the training coordinate extrema before the posterior draw and drops them from the result, and when newdata reaches past the training range it scales down the c of the gp() term by as much as the range grew, so brms rebuilds the boundary the model was fitted with. A prediction does not depend on which other rows share the call: chunked, fold-wise and single-call predictions agree, and predict_surface() does not depend on chunk_size. brms 2.23.0 and later store \(L\) and reuse it; there c is left alone and the two extra rows change nothing.

Predictions outside the training coordinate envelope are extrapolation, and a line in the log says so. A row further than \(L\) from the centre of the training coordinates on either axis is past the edge of the basis, where the approximate GP is an odd reflection of the fitted surface, so it is returned as NA (a column of NA with draws = TRUE) with a warning. The default boundary factor puts that edge well outside the training data.

Bayesian GP categorical predictors

A factor or character predictor is handed to brms with the levels the model was fitted with: the values that occur in the training rows (object$info$predictor_levels). A newdata factor that only lists an extra level, or a model fitted on a subset whose factor kept an unused level, is predicted as usual. A row whose value is not among the fitted levels has no prediction: it is returned as NA, the other rows are predicted, and one warning of class spatialkit_new_levels names the predictor, the levels and the number of rows. The result does not depend on which other rows share the call.

See also

predict_surface() to predict onto a grid, and area_of_applicability() to mark where the predictions apply.

Other fit methods: plot.spatial_fit(), print.spatial_fit(), spatial_fit-coef, spatial_fit-fitted, spatial_fit-residuals, summary.spatial_fit()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(60, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(60, 0, 1000),
             a = rnorm(60)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
pts$z <- 10 + 2 * pts$a + rnorm(60, 0, 0.3)
new <- pts[1:5, ]
new$z <- NULL                          # the response is not needed

rf <- fit_rf_model(pts, "z", "a", num_trees = 50, seed = 1)
predict(rf, newdata = new)
#> [1] 14.185278 10.109833 11.273408  9.993768  8.506111

gw <- fit_gwr_model(pts, "z", "a", bandwidth = 30)
str(predict(gw, newdata = new, se.fit = TRUE))
#> List of 5
#>  $ fit           : num [1:5] 14.62 9.88 11.35 10.07 8.56
#>  $ se.fit        : num [1:5] 0.1884 0.0784 0.0903 0.0768 0.1026
#>  $ se.pred       : num [1:5] 0.374 0.332 0.335 0.332 0.339
#>  $ residual.scale: num 0.323
#>  $ df            : num 46.8

# A point 4 km east of the data is beyond the reach of every kernel.  A
# handler totals the extrapolation warnings of several calls; the log
# lines still print (spatialkit_quiet() turns them off).
far <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x = 5.05e5, y = 5e6 + 500, a = 0),
                coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
total <- 0
withCallingHandlers(
  for (i in 1:2) predict(gw, newdata = far),
  spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation = function(w) {
    total <<- total + w$n_far
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
total
#> [1] 2
